prompt: A PM drafted this PRD section for a client's AI support-chat feature. Mark the lines that would cause trouble for the team or the client at sign-off.

task.prompt: A PM drafted this PRD section for a client's AI support-chat feature. Mark the lines that would cause trouble for the team or the client at sign-off.

segments.text: Problem: support agents spend about 40% of their time answering the same 20 order-status questions.
Goal: the chatbot should be fast and accurate.
segments.issue: Not measurable. State targets, e.g. p95 response under 3 s and an agreed accuracy bar on an evaluation set.

segments.text: Users: logged-in customers on web and the iOS/Android apps.
Non-goals: refunds and account deletion stay with human agents in this phase.
Requirement: the bot answers order-status questions using the client's Orders API.
Requirement: the bot should handle all other questions as well as possible.
segments.issue: Open-ended scope with no definition of done; list the intents in scope or move this to a later phase.

segments.text: Acceptance: verified by the client's QA team.
segments.issue: Says who, not what. Acceptance criteria must state the observable conditions to be met.

segments.text: Open question: does the Orders API expose delivery ETA? Owner: client tech lead, due 12 May.

prompt: Put these PRD sections in the order a reader should meet them, first at the top.

task.prompt: Put these PRD sections in the order a reader should meet them, first at the top.
task.explanation: A PRD argues from why to what: the problem and the measure of success come first, then who it is for, then what to build, how to verify it, and what is still undecided.

prompt: You are writing the PRD for a white-label loyalty app. In the discovery workshop the client's marketing lead said "we want gamification", the operations lead said "points must sync with the POS within a minute", and nobody mentioned offline use.

task.prompt: You are writing the PRD for a white-label loyalty app. In the discovery workshop the client's marketing lead said "we want gamification", the operations lead said "points must sync with the POS within a minute", and nobody mentioned offline use.

steps.question: How should "we want gamification" appear in the PRD?
options: As a requirement: "The app includes gamification"
Leave it out; it was only mentioned once
As an open question with an owner, until the client defines which mechanics and why
As a non-goal, since it is vague
steps.explanation: A vague wish written as a requirement becomes unbounded scope. Record it as an open question with an owner and a date.

steps.question: How should the POS sync be written?
options: "Points sync in real time"
"Points sync quickly with the POS"
"The POS integration works reliably"
"Points earned at the POS appear in the app within 60 seconds for 99% of transactions"
steps.explanation: A requirement needs a measurable threshold the team can test and the client can accept.

steps.question: Offline use was never discussed. What do you do?
options: Assume offline is needed and add it as a requirement
Assume it is not needed and say nothing
Add it to open questions and confirm with the client before sign-off
Ask the developers to decide
steps.explanation: Unstated assumptions become disputes at UAT. Surface them explicitly and get a decision.

prompt: A PRD review is due tomorrow and you have time for only some fixes. Rank these issues from most to least important to fix before the client signs.

task.prompt: A PRD review is due tomorrow and you have time for only some fixes. Rank these issues from most to least important to fix before the client signs.

items.label: No acceptance criteria for the payment-refund flow
Success metric "increase engagement" has no baseline or target
Out-of-scope list is missing, though the client keeps mentioning a web admin
Two requirements use different names for the same "merchant" entity
Section headings do not match the team's template

task.explanation: Missing acceptance criteria on money flows causes the most expensive disputes; an unmeasurable goal and an unstated boundary are next; naming and formatting are cheap to fix later.

prompt: These lines come from a functional spec for an AI receipt-scanning feature. Mark the lines that are not testable as written.

task.prompt: These lines come from a functional spec for an AI receipt-scanning feature. Mark the lines that are not testable as written.

segments.text: The user can photograph a receipt from the expense screen.

segments.issue: No threshold or evaluation method; nobody can say when it passes.

segments.text: Merchant, date and total are extracted and shown for review before saving.
On the agreed 200-receipt evaluation set, the total is correct on at least 95% of receipts.
If extraction fails, the user can type the fields manually.

segments.issue: Subjective; replace with concrete UX criteria such as steps or time to complete.

segments.text: Processing takes no longer than 5 seconds at p95 on a 4G connection.

prompt: Write the "Goals, non-goals and success metrics" section of a PRD for the feature in the context. Use bullets.

task.prompt: Write the "Goals, non-goals and success metrics" section of a PRD for the feature in the context. Use bullets.
task.context: Client: a regional pharmacy chain. Feature: AI prescription-refill reminders in their white-label app. Discovery notes: 30% of patients miss refills; the client wants fewer missed refills and fewer calls to stores. Phase 1 is push notifications only; SMS is a later phase. Pharmacists must still approve every refill. Baseline: 12,000 refill calls a month across stores.

rubric.label: Goals tied to the problem
rubric.description: States goals that follow from the missed-refill and call-volume problem, not features.

rubric.label: Measurable metrics
rubric.description: Each metric has the baseline and a target and a time frame, e.g. refill calls from 12,000 a month to a stated lower number within a stated period.

rubric.label: Clear non-goals
rubric.description: Names SMS as out of scope for phase 1 and keeps pharmacist approval with humans (no automated refill approval).

rubric.label: No invented facts
rubric.description: Does not invent decisions not in the notes; any target the notes do not give is marked as proposed or to be agreed.

task.sampleAnswer:
Goals
- Reduce missed prescription refills for app users.
- Reduce refill-related calls to stores.

Success metrics (targets proposed, to be agreed with the client)
- Missed-refill rate among app users: from 30% to 20% within 6 months of launch.
- Refill calls to stores: from 12,000 a month to 9,000 a month within 6 months.
- Reminder-to-refill-request conversion: tracked from launch, target set after the first month of data.

Non-goals (phase 1)
- SMS reminders (planned for a later phase).
- Automatic refill approval: every refill is still approved by a pharmacist.
- Changes to the in-store pharmacy system.

prompt: A developer asks why the PRD has a non-goals section at all. What is the best answer?

options: It lists features the team failed to estimate
It is where the PM puts requirements that the client may add later at no cost
It replaces the need for acceptance criteria
It records what the client agreed is out of scope, so expectations and change requests have a clear baseline
mcq.explanation: Non-goals make the boundary explicit. When the client later asks for an excluded item, the PRD shows it was out of scope, which turns an argument into a change request.

prompt: Who should own the answer to an open question in a PRD such as "Does the client's CRM allow write access via API?"

options: The PM, who should guess and move on
The whole team, discussed at stand-up
Nobody until development starts
A named person who can actually find out, usually on the client's side, with a due date
mcq.explanation: Open questions without an owner and a date stay open. The person with access to the answer (often the client's tech lead) owns it.

prompt: Midway through a sprint the client agrees a change to a requirement on a call. What should happen to the PRD?

options: Nothing; the PRD is frozen after sign-off
Update it with a version note and a link to the decision, and tell the team what changed
Rewrite the section silently so it reads cleanly
Start a new PRD for the change
mcq.explanation: A PRD is a living reference. Versioned changes linked to the decision keep the team and client aligned and preserve the audit trail for any commercial discussion.
